cells.tense: You are holding what needs holding right now, and it has not gone rigid in your hands.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: When someone close brings you something heavy, sit with it beside them for a minute, then say plainly where you stand. Both can be true at once.
cells.core:
You can take weight without going stiff, and in the places where fairness gets settled between two people, that steadiness does real work. Nothing here is clenched. You lift what needs lifting, you stay recognisable, and what you carry doesn't decide your shape.

What feeds this is contact that leaves both people whole. So when someone near you is under something, stand beside them rather than above or inside. Let what they are feeling reach you without making it yours to fix, then keep your own footing and say plainly what is yours. Both sides real at once, neither swallowed. You hold only what you agreed to hold, and you stay someone while you do it.
cells.sheetLine: You hold it steady, and you don't vanish into it.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: where the scales are set level again

cells.tense: You are bracing for a weight that hasn't landed yet, and the bracing has started to feel like the work.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Look at what you're holding for other people and rebalance one share. Hand back what belongs to them, then stop there — no lesson, no debt, nothing to collect.
cells.core:
The grip has outrun the need. You pick things up before they ask to be picked up, and hold them tighter than the situation calls for. From outside it reads as strength. From inside it is a fist kept closed against a future you cannot see arriving.

Fairness is the way back, and it stays small. Somewhere in your arms there is a portion that belongs to someone else. Set it back where it came from, without dressing it up as a lesson or a penalty. No ledger to keep. Just the load returned to its owner, and then you stop adjusting. An arm that was locked becomes an arm that moves.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding weight that isn't yours because you got there first.

cells.tense: You stood at that door a long time ago, and you are still standing in the same spot.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Choose something you've been carrying since bearing things stopped feeling safe, and set it down this week by deciding to. Leave your hands free of it and notice what's there.
cells.core:
Bearing gave out, and something in you decided the bearing itself was the dangerous part. So you stopped lifting, and where the strength used to sit there is an open, unguarded place. You are still at that door. Nothing you picked up back there has been set down deliberately; it still waits in your arms.

Letting go does what effort can't. Take one load that belongs to then rather than to your life now, and release it on purpose — deciding, not losing. Your hands stay free of it for a while. Nobody asks you to pick up anything new. Strength comes back by itself to a body no longer guarding a door it already walked through.
cells.sheetLine: You're still holding a door that closed behind you.

cells.tense: You are holding things level without noticing the hand that keeps them upright.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: Recall a moment you acted because you wanted to, not because it was owed, and tell yourself you chose it. Then move a little toward that again.
cells.core:
There is strength in you that you keep setting down as though it belonged to the room. People are steadier because you were there, and you would call that the situation being fine by itself. The hand keeping things level belongs to you, and you don't count it.

What brought you here was wanting something and moving toward it before you knew it would work. That pull is still in you, unattended. So look back at a moment you acted for no reason but wanting, and say plainly that you chose it. Then take a small step toward something the same shape this week, for nobody's benefit but your own. Light lands on what was cultivated first, and you have been cultivating without looking.
cells.sheetLine: The hand keeping things level is your own.

The reader's likely objection is that all four cells keep describing the same strength, which is the point: same capacity, four positions, and the ask each time is small enough to do without a reason. The ask survives being wrong because each one teaches something even if the read misses — a dropped condition, a fair share, a released grip, a chosen want. The sentence that serves the writer rather than the person is anything that would make the seat sound like earned wisdom; it is cut.
